The Vicissitudes of Imagery in Research and Clinical Use

Jerome Singer Ph.D.

Jerome Singer

Jerome L. Singer, Ph.D.
11 Eastern Drive
Ardsley, N.Y., 10502

Jerome Singer  

THE CHANGING FASHIONS of research and practical interests in imagery in psychology and psychiatry undoubtedly represent important trends in the evolution of sophisticated behavioral science. One might write a history of psychology and its crucial methodological problems built around the fate of the investigation of the image. Within just the past decade, there has been a proliferation in the variety and complexity of these methods of imagery investigation which, if added to the older European uses of such approaches, present a challenge to classification. Many of the methods are widely used now for group psychotherapy, encounter or sensitivity groups but the present paper focuses on the individual significance of imagery.

It seems appropriate to begin a survey of imagery methods by examining the use of imagery and fantasy in the more traditional psychoanalytic approaches. The latter have not often explicitly introduced imagery and fantasy as techniques because of the restrictions on directiveness and the necessity for permitting the unfolding of transference manifestations. Yet, in practice, classical analysis and some of its variants place a premium on the patient's capacity to generate imagery and to articulate this imagery verbally. As Wolstein 60 has shown, psychoanalysis never fully lost its original connection with hypnosis, wherein the patient is encouraged to produce vivid images or even hallucinations. Today we are closer to understanding the "mystery" of hypnosis imagery; we realize there is no mystery, thanks to the recent research of investigators such as Barber. 7

This is the first of two papers on imagery. The second, "The Theoretical and Practical Implications of Imagery, " will appear in a future issue of this Journal. This work was supported in part by U.S. Gov't. NIMH Grant #10956-06

IT IS INCREASINGLY evident that imagery is becoming widely utilized in a variety of therapy procedures that are based on very different conceptual orientations. Is there some common model that permits us to integrate this diverse material within a system more closely tied to operational definition and the possibilities of formal hypothesis-testing research? The purpose of the present paper is to map out one avenue that might lead to such a common vantage point. The major assumptions or relevant research literature underlying the suggestions offered here are available elsewhere (Richardson, 1969) ; (Singer, 1966) ; (Tomkins, 1962).

Towards a Cognitive Model for Imagery

One problem presented in the use of imagery by the Europeans and to a lesser extent by psychoanalytic groups is the tendency to regard the imagination as a realm through which one travels with a "guide" (Désoille, 1961), (1938). Recently, however, there has been increasing emphasis among behavioral scientists upon the important information-processing characteristic of man. In this frame of reference, the organism is seen as a set of interrelated systems built around the effective organization of experience and the production of plans and images that facilitate the screening and utilization of the multi-various cues and overall input from the external world.

Part II of a larger work on imagery and daydream techniques employed in psychotherapy. Part I, "The Vicissitudes of Imagery in Research and Clinical Use, " appeared in This Journal (Singer, 1971). These papers are based on research supported in part by U.S. Gov't. NIMH Grant # 10956-06.

Notes on Sullivan's Approach to the Science of Man

Ralph Crowley M.D.

Ralph Crowley

Ralph M. Crowley, M.D.
7 West 96th Street
New York, New York 10025

Ralph Crowley  

INTRODUCTION

SULLIVAN DEFINED PSYCHIATRY as the study of interpersonal relations. Although he regarded it as having relevance to a science of man, he believed it could not constitute alone a science of man. Nor did he feel that psychiatry could be scientific without the addition of the other social and behavioral sciences. He wrote quite clearly.

the elucidation of the fundamental characteristics of interpersonal relations ("personality processes") in the form of scientific laws requires the extended collaboration of investigators along many approaches (1964a, p. 28).

For the social sciences to be scientific, what psychiatry has learned is particularly useful, especially that body of information learned from the study of schizophrenic ways of life (1949, pp. 194–195). In fact, Sullivan might have preferred his point of view to be described as an approach to the sciences of human living, thus emphasizing process and change.

By defining psychiatry as the study of interpersonal relations, Sullivan regarded psychiatry as an expanding science concerned with the kinds of events and processes in which the psychiatrist participates while being an observant psychiatrist (1953, p. 13). But what can the psychiatrist observe? Only activity in the public mode can be observed, and that part of activity in the private mode that is communicable and thus made observable. Such activity consists of events in interpersonal fields which include the psychiatrist.

This essay is based on a presentation to The Committee on Psychoanalysis as a Science of Man at the William Alanson White Institute, New York City, on October 24, 1970.

DR. SZALITA in this paper makes a plea for a broader life and professional experience for the analyst of the individual. Disheartened by analyses in which one of the outcomes was divorce, surprised by her patient being different under circumstances different from the analytic situation, she has moved to family study, group study, and Kibbutz study. Her goal is quite clear—she wants to narrow the gap between conceptual framework and concrete experience. This is a task well understood by particularly Sullivan and Fromm and Thompson.

I feel she would agree that family interviews are only one way of narrowing this gap. Other ways are the reading of great literature—wherein the wisdom of the centuries and the interplay between different people are portrayed—the viewing of drama and the leading of a full life by the analyst. Most analysts spend most of their free time with analysts. There is a whole world out there with different kinds of people!

Dr. Szalita is also saying that the quality of presence is heightened by the use of these ancillary interviews. The quality of presence is composed of factors involving attention and observation. She shows that issues around interaction—interpersonal communication, both verbal and nonverbal—are heightened by the family or couple interview. She makes the necessary point that clarifying the parataxic distortions in the me-you are not enough to clarify parataxic or characterological problems with other people in other situations.

Underlying the entire paper are a number of attitudes that are Dr. Szalita. She makes an eloquent passionate plea for the acceptance of differences among members of a family unit. No simple egalitarian, she abjures premature separation of the young from the family. She is in favor of freedom with the proviso that responsibility go along pari passu with freedom. She rediscovers the significance of people being different with different people—of the fact that it is not enough to assume that all of the patient's attitudes will be transferred onto the analyst's personality. She points out the importance of interpersonal communication. She wants there to be a leader in the family. No faddist, she wants family interviews to facilitate, not supplant individual therapy. She does this all with a clarity, astuteness, and compassion which certainly bode well for her quality of presence. I suspect family interviewing is only one route by which she has developed it.

Comments and Criticisms

To the Editors:

In his unemotional paper on a highly emotionally loaded subject for which he deserves greatest praise, C. C. Dahlberg mentions the infantile grandiosity that is blatant in the therapist who ventures to cure the patient through sexual intimacy ["Sexual Contact between Patient and Therapist, " This Journal, Vol. 6, No. 2 (Spring 1970)]. However, Dahlberg fails to see this grandiosity in McCartney, whom he quotes but treats with too much protectiveness. In the article referred to by Dahlberg, McCartney claims to "have conducted over fifteen hundred psychoanalyses … with an average of 89 hours" over forty years. Assuming that he worked 365 days per year, this represents ten patient-sessions per day, which McCartney claims "represents 26 per cent of all the psychiatric patients seen." He thus must have seen an additional thirty patients per day 365 days per year!

This raises the question of how many patients McCartney, who was sixty-seven or sixty-eight years old when he wrote this article, treated daily in accordance with their sexual needs. It also raises the question as to what he did with male patients who might need therapeutic sexual intervention. It thus seems clear that all justifications of sexual contact between patient and therapist must be put into their proper place as rationalizations and denial.

I am wondering whether psychopathic tendencies do not play a part in therapists' sexual acting out. A former patient of mine in her twenties had first been seduced by her former therapist, who was married and had a child. Then the therapist found another female patient of his to informally adopt his mistress and support her through college. Of course, the adoptive mother knew nothing, and was to know nothing, of the affair between her therapist and her adoptive daughter. Furthermore, the therapist employed his mistress (after discontinuing her treatment) as secretary, in which capacity she was typing up material concerning other patients.

Dr. Ortmeyer replies:

Dr. Brandt's comments are appreciatively received. There appears no strong disagreement, rather an affirmation of the "we-self." To carry the understanding of we-self and I-self through all developmental phases is a point well-taken; and hopefully is the subject of future papers. This paper focused on two crucial periods of development of the we-self: the first months of life with the mother, when the symbiotic ties are present and then begin to dissolve; at the time of language acquisiton when words begin to be used in correct grammatical context, via imitation, but the implicit meanings may not be consensually validated ones.

The conceptual formulation of "identity" is certainly prominent in the field, particularly in the wiritings of Freud, neo-Freudians, and Erikson. I prefer the conceptual context of "self" and "self-system" as put forth by Sullivan.— D.H.O.

[[RunningHead]]

Reply to Dr. Fiasche

John Hartman Ph.D.

John Hartman

John Hartman  

DR. FIASCHE'S DISCUSSION of my paper was most interesting. I am pleased that it stimulated such a wide-ranging and lively discussion. There are several points of that discussion to which I must reply in order to clarify some important issues.

The first has to do with the question of diagnostic appraisal, which Dr. Fiasche feels I made incorrectly. There was a great reluctance on the part of the hospital staff and the first therapist to see the patient as schizophrenic. I believe that she was schizophrenic and that the course of her therapy, with the gradual uncovering of world destruction fantasies and distorted object relations, bore out this appraisal. I meant to convey a description of ego functioning by using the term schizophrenic as I am not particularly fond of diagnostic labels. I have found Bellak's description of ego functioning in schizophrenia1 useful in this regard. Perhaps I could have described this better, but I assumed that the material would convey the psychotic nature of Miss A's functioning. I think that Dr. Fiasche's statements about "psychopathic defenses of hysterical and epileptoid nature" are incorrect, quite misleading, and arbitrary appraisals that only confuse the issues I raised. I am reminded of Rudolf Ekstein's remark, (in replying to comments on patients in his Childhood Psychosis Project) that whenever patients improve, people feel they could not have been psychotic in the first place. It is as if there was no therapy done, just diagnostic error.

Dr. Fiasche believes that I changed a theoretical model into an ideology.

1See Chapter one in Bellak, L., Schizophrenia: A Review of the Syndrome. New York: Logos Press, 1958.28

33 West 60th Street

Sanford Sherman  

DR. SZALITA'S PAPER shows her incisive impatience with flabby thought and empty concept—the inverse of which is her highly disciplined, really marvelously uncluttered way of thinking and expressing herself.

I wish to review a few of the themes she elucidated:

One can be comfortably different only when one can be similar to those around one and also allow the other to see things differently so as not to assume that there is only one way of looking at things.

Isolation and pseudo-independence are often confused with development of true individuality.

To take care of another has been conceived as a loss, not a gain, by many patients ending their psychotherapy.

The analyst can become aware that the analysis of transference in the analytic situation does not include the whole variety of such possible releasers (i.e., in the interaction with other people) which may precipitate repetition-compulsion.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Reply to Drs. Schechter and Wolstein

Ralph Crowley M.D.

Ralph Crowley

Ralph Crowley  

Dr. Schechter discusses two conceptions of Sullivan's; namely, "interpersonal relations" and "parataxic." In doing so, he has developed and amplified what I wrote. By his detailed explications, he clarifies the meaning and significance of these two concepts. While Schechter deliberately omitted from his discussion reference to the relevance of these concepts to a science of man, his very lucidity facilitates understanding of their relevance. How? Schechter notes that the concept of interpersonal relations refers both to structure and process, and both to the intrapsychic and to behavioral interactions between individuals. With a term that refers to both at once, Sullivan avoids the artificial disassociation of these inextricably interpenetrating phenomena, making possible a novel approach to the science of man. This overcomes the difficulties of the overstructuralization of the Freudian superego-ego-id theory. It offers a superior, more flexible approach to the science of man, which includes both process and structure, both situation and person.

Dr. Wolstein, on the other hand, maintains that Sullivan's approach is untenable because his is a theory of interpersonal relations without individuality. How can such a theory possibly have value, he asks repetitiously and rhetorically. He gives no evidence that a theory including the concept of unique individuality is the gainer by its inclusion. He makes it sound like some crucial and fatal omission to have a theory of interpersonal relations without a concept of a "real self." Wolstein mistakenly equates unique individuality or self with the concept of a separate person. I agree it is unthinkable to have a theory of interpersonal relations without some concept of a separate or individual person. But what is a person? I do not believe that one needs to postulate that person and unique individuality or "real self" are synonymous.

WHAT IS AVAILABLE to the psychoanalyst for analysis is verbal. Typically what is analyzed is not the patient's dream but the report of the dream, the report of his inner experience. 3 Noverbal gestures figuring in the discourse between patient and therapist are also translated into verbal imagery, by one or the other, before they too are subject to analytic scrutiny. The language of experience is a transformation of imagery or fantasy into verbal interchange.

One might infer, then, that the structuring of unconscious forces is revealed in the structure of language. 2 The total language—communicative gestures, verbal and nonverbal—is the representation of these forces. When our patients relate their histories, they describe not so much the actual events as dreams or desires betrayed. Their verbal accounts refer to definitions of the self, the other, and the relationship between the two—as much as they do to real events. Words or their equivalents are containers of relationships between the speaker and some needed property of the object contained.

Through dreams, poetry, and fiction, what is out of awareness becomes personified dramatically. Interactions occur between fictive figures who, though moving with autonomy, are experienced as being parts of our own psyches. We respond with acclaim to that artist whose knowledge and skill articulate for us all passions, all dimensions of human life, and all of the mysteries of human existence with its possibility for change. Any play or novel can be read by the psychoanalyst as a dream (not the author's) with typical structure, plot, sequences, imagery, conflicts, and resolutions.

The Analyst as Philosopher

Ralph Crowley M.D.

Ralph Crowley

Ralph M. Crowley, M.D.
7 West 96th Street, 2E
New York, N.Y. 10025

Ralph Crowley  

Rollo May: Love and Will.
New York: W. W. Norton, 1969. 352 pages, $7.95.

ALFRED ADLER USED TO SAY about a unified personality, or as we call it today, one's identity, that the self-constructed personality is fiction. 1, p. 9 Rollo May, in asserting the thesis that man's task in life is to transcend what he is, to create a self out of the raw material at hand, readily admits to man's tendency to self-deception, but insists on his need for myths to live a meaningful life. May not only discusses at great length, love and will, which gives this large, classically erudite tome its title, but fills a broad canvas with a philosophy of man, in the development of which a theory of personality is implicit. In so doing, he carries on Adler's emphasis on the role of social interest in one's style of life; for social interest, or ethics, according to May, is based on man's psychology,

the capacities of a human being to transcend the concrete situation of the immediate self-oriented desire and to live in the dimensions of the past and future, and in terms of the welfare of the persons and groups upon which his own fulfillment ultimately depends. 10, p. 25

This achievement apparently involves, either in or outside of therapy, the bringing together of wish, will, and decision. For, May tells us,

decision creates a pattern of acting and living, which is empowered by wishes, asserted by will and is responsible to and responsible for the significant other persons who are important to oneself in the realizing of long term goals. 10, p. 25

Sullivan leaps to mind immediately with his remark about being "born with something of this power motive in us." 15, p. 6

[[RunningHead]]

A Time to Heal

William Goldfarb, M.D., Ph.D., Irving Mintz, M.S.W., and Katherine W. Stroock, A.B.

Zira De Fries M.D.

Zira De Fries

Zira De Fries  

New York: International Universities Press, 1969, 158 pages, $5.00.

A Time to Heal is a happy example of the art that therapy can and should be when superimposed on a theoretical substratum and practiced by skilled technicians. In this slender and readily readable volume on the treatment of childhood schizophrenia, the theoretical formulations and the practical implications of such theory are spelled out in a series of vignettes that, when added up, delineate the disordered life patterns of the schizophrenic child and the manner in which a devoted and disciplined staff attempts to alter such aberrant patterns. The authors use the term "corrective socialization" and it is this, in the most literal sense, that they appear to accomplish with a number of the children in treatment in the Ittleson Center for Child Research (where they have been engaged in research and treatment of schizophrenic children for more than fifteen years). Their emphasis is upon providing a milieu in which the entire staff is geared to the understanding of the individual child's pathology and to rectifying this by gentle but direct challenging of each child's persistent needs to perpetuate his self-defeating behavior.

The authors envision the schizophrenic child as being deficient in adaptive functioning; he lacks proper tools for perceiving, ordering, and manipulating reality; he fails miserably in predicting the impact of his behavior on others because of his limited self-awareness. They see the "educative correction of these fundamental lacks as the sine qua non of treatment" and point out that "the most important method of achieving correction lies in the process of human interaction"—hence, their term corrective socialization.

Having briefly established their theoretical framework, they proceed in the remainder of the book to illuminate how they tackle, in the structured setting of the institution, instances of a range of behavior specific to the psychopathology of the schizophrenic child, such as defective orientation in time and space, lack of awareness of boundaries between self and others, illusions of omnipotence, and defensive withdrawal.

[[RunningHead]]

Dr. Werner Schwidder

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski  

WERNER SCHWIDDER died on September 2, 1970 while attending the International Forum of Psychoanalysis in Madrid.

I knew Werner Schwidder over a period of ten years and found him to be a man of strong personal appeal and genuine human and professional integrity. While the number of contacts I had with him was limited, we established a strong personal rapport. I was his guest at Tiefenbrunnen on several occasions and also saw a great deal of him during meetings of the Forum.

The idea of an International Forum had originated with Dr. Schwidder, and I had the good fortune to work with him on this project from the beginning. He had contacted the William Alanson White Society expressing the hope that a new kind of international scientific cooperation could be started after World War II, one that would go beyond the framework of the International Psychoanalytic Society. There were great difficulties in getting the venture under way. Personalities, psycho-politics and training backgrounds became issues.

A scholarly, hard-working man with a touch of sensitive humor, Werner Schwidder was often saddened by the pettiness of colleagues in his attempts to promote an effective international dialogue. His personality and dedication were recognized by all. He served terms as president of both the orthodox group and the neo-orthodox group in which he was active in Germany.

Schwidder was born in Berlin on November 9, 1917, studied medicine in Berlin and Leipzig, and began psychoanalytic training during World War II, in 1941. Later, he became a training and supervisory analyst and a member of the Institute in Berlin, from which he had been graduated. He worked in various hospitals and eventually became Director of the Institute for Psychological Disorders in Children and Adolescents. From 1951 until his death, he worked in Tiefenbrunnen, from 1965 as Director of the hospital. He was appointed a professor at the University of Goettingen in 1968.

218

[[RunningHead]]

Comments and Criticisms

To the Editor:

In his excellent paper on "The We-Self of Identical Twins [ This Journal, Volume 6, No. 2], D. H. Ortmeyer could have more strongly emphasized the specific developmental problems encountered by identical twins. The development of the self is closely related to that of a sense of identity and uniqueness. This development is made more difficult for identical twins than for anyone else by the fact that the identical twin has in his environment someone who looks like his mirror image.

It has been observed that as a rule identical twins recognize later than other children their mirror image as a reflection of themselves. Furthermore, not only the mother (whom Ortmeyer mentions) but also everyone else confuses the identical twins and thus inhibits their identity development. The higher incidence of schizophrenia among identical twins may just as well be due to these impediments in identity development, which lead to the we-self, as to the supposed identical genetic material.

As to Ortmeyer's speculation "that recall of very early childhood events may be a construction based upon the later comments of others rather than a reporting of the early immediate experience" (footnote on page 134), J. Piaget1 relates exactly such a pseudo-memory of his and discusses why he does not believe that true memories of events of the first three years of life exist.—LEWIS W. BRANDT, Ph.D., Regina, Canada.

1In Play, Dream and Imitation in Childhood (New York: Norton, 1951).221

Kingsley Hall: The Politics of Madness

Morton Schatzman M.D.

Morton Schatzman

Morton Schatzman, M.D.
50 Courthope Road
London NW3, England

Morton Schatzman  

THERE IS REASON believe that seeing someone as mentally ill, labeling him mentally ill, and treating him as if he were mentally ill makes him more likely to act as if he were mentally ill.

When people think someone is mentally ill, they treat him differently. They expect him to think, feel, and act strangely. They regard what he says and does as signs of illness. To tell someone with a physical disease like a tumor that he is ill does not affect the course of the disease, as far as we know; to tell someone he is mentally ill affects him and can lead him to enact his idea of mental illness.

To refuse to label certain experiences and behavior as ill is not to fail to see they may be unusual. However, what is regarded as odd or bothersome in some social circles may not be in others. Many "mentally ill" persons need time, space, and encouragement to do and be more than they have been allowed before.

Three psychiatrists in England, Drs. David Cooper, Aaron Esterson, and R. D. Laing, proposed to make this possible. With some co-workers and friends they founded the Philadelphia Association Ltd., a charity that has sponsored one household, and affiliated itself with some others, where people who had been or could be diagnosed as "mentally ill" have lived outside mental hospitals.

They chose to drop the medical model for that class of behavior for which no physical cause has been found and which is called mental illness.

Adapted from "Madness and Morals, " an article published in Counter Culture: The Creation of an Alternative Society, edited by Joseph Berke (London: Peter Owen, 1970).

Harry Bone, Ph.D.

Seymour Fuchsman

Seymour Fuchsman

Seymour Fuchsman  

I MET HARRY more than twenty years ago. I don't remember exactly when, but he, and the meeting, remain fixed forever. I was asking him to be my teacher. I wasn't bargaining on getting a dear friend.

I started conventionally enough. I had done this before. But Harry was never conventional. He had a way of involving himself with you so that you knew something important was happening beyond the case. He had himself been through too much to believe old mumbo-jumbos and he was not going to pass those on. So things had to make sense; and he made sense. One time I found myself working so hard to impress him that I was in danger of losing my patient. Harry simply said, "We'll work on another one." No criticism. No dissection of what was wrong. That was not the time. He knew, I think, before Skinner, that punishment doesn't enhance learning. At any rate, he was passionately devoted to growth rather than alteration; and he knew how to create the conditions for growth. He spoke of it as the difference between horticulture and carpentry, and he was able to teach, perhaps by example, how to nurture people rather than reconstruct them, how to help them to their own essence rather than to some psychoanalytic model of what they should be.

He had an abiding distrust of models just as he had an abiding faith in people, if only they dared find themselves. He himself never gave up that personal struggle. If there was anyone who could add to his knowledge of himself, Harry sought him out. It mattered not what their status was, nor for that matter, their geography. It was not long ago that he was willing to travel to the Pacific end of Canada where Fritz Perls might have had something to offer. His readiness to search high and low often confounded the real and would-be elder statesmen, but it was an inspiration to his students.

Harry was a man of ideas, and his inquiries never stopped. He was never in my house without looking through my books, not to see what I was reading, but to see what he might have missed. He could always find something to intrigue him. It might be a large volume by Bertrand Russell or a small one on Chassidism.

Notes on "Problems of Creativity"

Joanne Greenberg

Joanne Greenberg

Joanne Greenberg
Route 3, Box 321
Golden, Colorado 80401

Joanne Greenberg  

To the Editor:

It is murder to take a stand on this at all. For whom am I speaking? Creative people? Arrogant and, of course dishonest! Myself? Fine, but who the hell is she? And there is the terrible urge here to be flip, because Dr. Storr and many others can't seem to figure out who's got the problem, we or they. I think my epigraph sets up another basic problem, really, and that is, who defines the creative person, and creativity? God knows, there is more bilge spoken on that subject than the mind can compass. Girls in Women's Lib. talk about how you have to get out of the house to be creative. (I think they confuse creativity with non-repetitiveness. What a piece of hot hot news I have for them!)

What bothers me is that writers and painters and musicians, some of whom have no understanding of the joys of a world of reality apart from the esthestic pleasure of producing poetry or music, have to get help from doctors who may doubt the "sanity" of this activity. It also saddens me that my words will be of no help in that case. J.G.

A writer whose work is not published is a bum.

A writer whose work is published is creative.

A writer who is dead is a master. If he dies before the age of thirty-five, he

is a genius.

IT IS FUN to be able to read an article and just stand on the sidelines and throw rocks, or in my case, pebbles. It beats having to sit down and write the article one's self. It is an interesting article—"Problems of Creativity." Since I am published, I am creative, but Dr. Storr didn't hit any of my problems until later in piece—what he starts out talking about are his problems (his and Freud's and psychiatry's)

Some Issues in Community Mental Health—Psychoanalysis and Community Psychiatry: Confrontation or Collaboration?

C. Aldrich M.D.

C. Aldrich

C. Knight Aldrich, M.D.
Department of Psychiatry New Jersey College of Medicine and Dentistry
100 Bergen Street
Newark, N.J. 07103

C. Aldrich  

AT FIRST SIGHT psychoanalysis and community psychiatry seem to be natural enemies. Psychoanalysis is the epitome of private practice psychiatry; community psychiatry is really a new term for public health psychiatry. As community psychiatry has grown to become a major force in American psychiatry, confrontation between these two opposites would appear to be as inevitable as that between free private enterprise and socialism, and any unforced collaboration would seem unlikely.

Contributions of Psychoanalysis to Community Psychiatry

Nevertheless, there has been collaboration of a kind between community psychiatry and psychoanalysis. Regardless of the emphasis it places on social factors in mental illness and on social action, community psychiatry must also be concerned with individual patients, and psychoanalysis provides by far the most comprehensive framework for understanding individual psychology yet devised. Furthermore, although some psychoanalysts have perceived the community component of psychiatry only as a threat to the purity of psychoanalysis, others have contributed substantially to community psychiatry. They have contributed a basic understanding of unconscious mechanisms and a deeper awareness of the individual as he participates in his social systems. They have helped workers in the field of community psychiatry to understand resistance, and to tolerate hostility on the part of others. They have helped to adapt to community settings concepts of transference and countertransference.

The three papers that follow are based on a discussion of current developments in community psychiatry at the regular meeting of the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Society held on February 12, 1970.

The authors were given the opportunity to revise or expand their oral presentations.

Angel Fiasche  

DR. HARTMAN'S PAPER is an attempt to clarify the vicissitudes undergone by the dyadic psychotherapeutic process when a third element is added to its dynamics—whether that be an institution, a seminar, a case conference, or a supervisory situation. This is a most relevant and valuable work for psychoanalysis and psychotherapy since it makes evident the existence of collateral factors that influence the course of treatment. William Caudill (1954) did an exhaustive study that demonstrated that, for a hospitalized patient, the therapeutic process operates not only via the psychotherapeutic sessions but also through the interaction with institutional life, the latter interfering, as often as not, with the dynamic interaction of individual treatment.

The author focuses his study on a specific aspect of this phenomenon: the understanding of the conflict created by the addition of a third variable to the analytic situation, in the dynamics of transference, countertransference, their course, and resolution. With Dr. Hartman's patient, this third element emerges from the dynamics of the case conference.

It is important to point out that the references cited are superfluous save for the paper by Searles (1955). The works of Guiora and associates, Brody, and Whitman, are neither relevant to the author's purpose nor do they refer to the same phenomenon. One cannot regard a learning seminar and clinical case conference for residents and students as dealing with the same problems and dynamics of group process. The interests at stake, the attitudes, the degree of dependency, the quality of the rivalry—all the phenomenology and dynamics—have psychological nuances and intensities that make comparison impossible.

In this respect I believe that Dr. Hartman has based his report exclusively on the work of Dr. Searles. Using his theoretical framework, Dr. Hartman attempts to demonstrate that the emotional interaction between the members of the case conference and himself in his role of presenter allowed him to become aware of aspects of non-resolved countertransference during treatment that had interfered with the therapeutic process.

THERE HAVE BEEN surprisingly few studies of case conferences in clinical settings. Each week members of hospital, institute, and clinic staffs "present" patients and treatment plans to colleagues and superiors in almost ritualized group events. These conferences represent a vast untapped source of information about the group processes operating among staff personnel and also may reveal previously unconscious interaction between the therapist-presenter and the patient. This paper describes an experience with a case conference in which a previously unrecognized dilemma in the psychotherapy of a young schizophrenic woman was played out in the course of the presentation and discussion.

Several authors have discussed the case conference in terms of group dynamics. Whitman (1956) used both ratings and observation techniques in his analysis of a psychiatric staff conference. He suggested that conferences were a source of emotional satisfaction for staff personnel and therefore a rich and complex source of group interaction. He used Bion's (1961) scheme for understanding group process—that despite the group's stated learning purpose, members find themselves seeking to fulfill fight-flight, pairing, or dependency needs. A Brief Introduction to Jacques Lacan

Octave Mannoni Ph.D.

Octave Mannoni

Octave Mannoni, Ph.D.
35, avenue Ferdinand Buisson
Paris 16e, France

Octave Mannoni  

EVEN THE MOST OUTSPOKEN critics of Jacques Lacan recognize today that he has done the most to contribute to progress in and to a probing study of psychoanalytic theory in France. He has brought about a renewal of interest in analytic doctrine remarkable for its trenchant and far-reaching questions. Before giving a short sketch of Lacan's basic positions, a brief historical review will be useful.

A professional psychoanalytic society has existed in France since 1925, and the overall emphasis has tended to be on clinical practice. French psychoanalysts, therapeutically minded, practiced "by the rules, " so to speak, without delving into the theoretical reasoning behind their therapeutic achievements. The theoretical reasoning remained a kind of happy mystery for them. They were therefore ignored by the French intelligentsia, who long ago did indeed realize what was radically new in Freud's discoveries. The psychoanalysts, however, were content in their isolation.

In 1952 a schism concerning recruitment and training of psychoanalysts developed. Half of the analysts, most of them younger people, followed the concepts of Lacan, of whom little was known at the time. Thus he was able to organize the teaching in his dissenting group, and he turned toward a probing study of Freud's theoretical works. The return to Freud, the return of Freud into psychoanalysis became the rallying cry.

At first Lacan's group systematically studied Freud's texts.

Translated from the French by I. Ilton and A. H. Feiner.

The Relevance of Family Interviewing for Psychoanalysis

Alberta Szalita M.D.

Alberta Szalita

Alberta B. Szalita, M.D.
251 Central Park Wast
New York, N.Y. 10024

Alberta Szalita  

FAMILY INTERVIEWING, or family therapy as some prefer to call it, is by now a well-established, fashionable modality of psychotherapy and, for analysts engaged in such work, one of the many branches of applied psychoanalysis. As yet there is no adequate formulation of the meaning of "applied psychoanalysis, " for it is difficult indeed to define what psychoanalytic training adds to the practice of social and community psychiatry, and to what degree and precisely why a psychoanalyst may contribute more to such programs than analogous professionals without such training.

The recent interest in family development and family life, as well as the sprouting up of various forms of group therapy, seems to reflect a trend against isolation and loneliness, deeply felt by a large segment of the population, young and old. Some view this as a trend against individualism, which, I think, is a misconception. Stress is placed on independence in the sense of living alone as soon as one is out of school, or before finishing college, and on earning a living; but, important as that might be, it does not necessarily develop individuality. All too often it contributes to isolation and a kind of pseudo-independence.

Major patterns of contemporary social change seem to reflect a reaction to this pseudo-individualistic trend of recent decades. And I am not certain that we, as psychoanalysts, were not caught up in the same process and have not contributed to this social malaise rather than helping to cure it.

A paper delivered before the William Alanson White Society, New York City, on December 14, 1970.

Interpersonal Relations without Individuality

Benjamin Wolstein Ph.D.

Benjamin Wolstein

Benjamin Wolstein, Ph.D.
2 West 67th Street
New York, N.Y. 10023

Benjamin Wolstein  

AS COMMENTARY on Dr. Ralph Crowley's very balanced, carefully stated review of Sullivan's critique of the notion of unique individuality, I call attention to a long-neglected, unsolved problem in the interpersonal perspective. Dating back at least twenty-five years, that problem has at least two noteworthy aspects: (1) the absence of individuality from interpersonal relations and (2) the diagnosis of unique individuality as delusion.

(1) While it is false, as Dr. Crowley indicates, to propose that Sullivan "denied the existence or the reality of the unique individual, " it is, nonetheless, true that he nowhere affirmed its existence and reality as part of the study of interpersonal relations, either. For, as Dr. Crowley continues, "He believed and stated that there was no way to study it, by the methods of science …" By so construing both the methods of science and the uniqueness of individual human psyches as mutually exclusive, however, his is clearly an interpersonal relations without individuality.

In Conceptions, Sullivan was very emphatic about it: "The unique individuality of the other fellow need never concern us as scientists. It is a great thing in our wives and our children." As though to say that what goes on between us and our wives and our children is outside his study of interpersonal relations and, therefore, need never concern us as scientists.

Psychoanalysis, the Black Community and Mental Health

Hugh Butts M.D.

Hugh Butts

Hugh F. Butts, M.D.
16 East 79th Street
New York; N.Y. 10021

Hugh Butts  

THOREAU WROTE: "No way of thinking or doing, however ancient, can be trusted without proof. What everybody echoes or in silence passes by as true today may turn out to be falsehood tomorrow, mere smoke of opinion, which some had trusted for a cloud that would sprinkle fertilizing rain on their fields." This statement from Walden is extremely applicable to the theme of Dr. Aldrich's paper, and the falsehoods he has challenged.

While Dr. Aldrich's presentation is salutary, I would like to deal with an aspect alluded to, but not elaborated by him—namely, Psychoanalysis, Community Psychiatry, and the Black Community. Three issues are germane to this consideration:

1. In what ways has psychoanalysis failed to demonstrate its relevance and applicability to the black community? How can this relevance and applicability be provided?

2. How can psychoanalysis make a meaningful contribution to social issues and legislative-political considerations and decisions affecting the lives of millions of black ghetto denizens?

3. How can psychoanalysis purge itself of the group-related paranoia that has resulted in the over-evaluation and acceptance of those belonging to the analytic ilk, while regarding as inadequate, sinister, and different those who are different, and eventually rejecting them?

I use the term psychoanalysis not in reference to formal psychoanalytic treatment, but instead to psychoanalysis as a method of investigating and understanding mental illness (and health), and the utilization of analytic principles in the service, prevention, and amelioration of ghetto mental illness.

The Psychoanalyst, the Community and the Schools

Gerald Emmet M.D.

Gerald Emmet

Gerald M. Emmet, M.D.
315 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10025

Gerald Emmet  

MANY PSYCHOANALYSTS are extremely concerned about the political and environmental turmoil which surrounds them. They are struggling to find avenues for activities that might reconcile their need for social action with their professional functions. The field of Community School Psychiatry offers a possible model for working towards such a goal.

During a period of rapid social upheaval, institutions alter their goals and structure, and new professions seem to spring up overnight in order to keep pace. They may develop as an extension of preexisting professional role models. Two institutions, each struggling to maintain its own viability, may also find it worthwhile (or even necessary) to create a new service either as an amalgam of their separate areas of expertise, or arising de novo out of their collaboration.

Today, educational institutions are undergoing major revisions in basic concepts and techniques. They are also questioning their ability to respond to community directives and to be more alert to the specific needs of children in impoverished or minority groups. Similarly, the mental health professions are in a period of flux, not only as a result of self-exploration by the professional community, but also as a response to pressure from the population they serve. There is a move away from individually oriented psychotherapies to techniques that can respond to broader needs. It is at such a moment historically that both professional groups are collaborating in defining how best to collaborate. Thus, the extent to which they see themselves either as responsive to community needs, or as participants with the community in a joint undertaking, determines the kind of relationship that will be established.

The field of Community School Psychiatry is difficult to define.

153

Comments and Criticisms on "The We-Self of Identical Twins"

Henry Fox M.D.

Henry Fox

Henry M. Fox, M.D.
Harvard, Medical School
Cambridge, Mass.

Henry Fox  

To the Editors:

I was tremendously interested in Dr. Dale Ortmeyer's recent article on twinship [ This Journal, volume 6, No. 2]. His emphasis on complementarity is very stimulating and certainly corresponds to our clinical observations. We have been observing twins for quite a number of years as part of a psychophysiological study.

Our clinical material includes about twenty pairs of monozygotic and ten pairs of dizygotic male twins of college age (many of them undergraduates at Harvard). They were, of course, going throught the phase of post-adolescence. Our observations have included about nine recorded interviews (about an hour each) on each of the subjects which were subsequently typed. We have also carried out studies of the metabolic end-products of steroid metabolism in the form of 17-ketosteroids and 17-hydroxycorticosteroids in urine samples (about thirty-five 24-hour urine samples for each subject).

I must admit I had not realized how difficult it would be to apply any existing concepts concerning linguistics to our material. We have, however, felt sure that we can only get an answer by making full use of the implications of post-adolescence. The fact that these are college boys (often at the same college) would seem to make the shift from emphasis on motor activity to articulate intellectual communication of particular importance. But here again we are in an area where the complexities of twinship have to be considered in every possible way, including the urge for polarization as part of the process of establishing individuality and the way in which the pattern of complementarity, as Dr. Ortmeyer has so well described it, becomes revised.

134

Two of Sullivan's Conceptions

David Schecter M.D.

David Schecter

David E. Schecter, M.D.
6 Claremont Rd.
Scarsdale, N.Y. 10583

David Schecter  

DR. CROWLEY'S STIMULATING paper focuses on the relation of several of Sullivan's conceptions to the development of a science of man. I will here limit myself to a discussion of two of these conceptions without immediate reference to their relevance to a science of man.

I

Dr. Crowley has fulfilled a much-needed service in elaborating on what is meant by interpersonal relations. Although Sullivan's theoretical thrust was to break through the notion of an encapsulated psyche driven by its own finite energies, he also made clear that he was not only concerned about events occurring outside the process of "mentation" characterizing a given individual. So it is that "interpersonal relations" is a most complex conception which, at one level of abstraction, can refer to observable behavioral interactions between individuals while, at another level, it refers to "intrapsychic" symbolic representations of interpersonal events.

The Changing Language of Self

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
45 East End Avenue
New York, N.Y. 10028

Gerard Chrzanowski  

Frederick J. Hoffman: Samuel Beckett: The Language of Self. New York: E. P. Dutton, 1964. 177 pages, (paperback) $1.50.

THE AUTHOR of this slender volume, a professor of modern literature at the University of California whose earlier works were devoted to Gertrude Stein, Freudianism, the literary mind, and the novel of the 1920s, has written a sophisticated essay on Beckett's epistemological inquiry into human existence. His discussion starts with Dostoevsky's "Notes from the Underground" and continues through the late nineteenth century with selected examples from Turgenev, Gogol, and Goncharov. Hoffman leads us to the twentieth century with brief references to Kafka and Beckett's friend, James Joyce. My commentary is concerned with Dostoevsky's, Kafka's, and Beckett's conceptions of the self and how they relate to those of Freud and Sullivan.

Dostoevsky's Underground Man

Hoffman initially presents a tripartite analysis of Dostoevsky's concept. It identifies three levels of awareness pertaining to the self: (a) as a self-conscious actor; (b) as a reflected appraisal of itself in the eyes of others (the observer and the observed); and (c) as a representation of a rational, Aristotelian type of logic. Dostoevsky's underground man is both sentimental and cynical. He watches himself in the mirror of his mind and assumes to some degree the dual role of actor and observer. The underground man as depicted by Dostoevsky is an ambiguous person suffering from "the disease of consciousness." Much of his energy is invested in assuming the part of the observer without having a reliable platform for his observations.

"We"

Aurelia Levi Ph.D.

Aurelia Levi

Aurelia Levi, Ph.D.
440 Riverside Drive
New York, N.Y. 10027

Aurelia Levi  

THE ATTRACTIVE young man of good character, good parts, good family, and good expectations, who nevertheless takes dismayingly great pleasure in the company of chambermaids and such, is quaintly familiar to us, irrelevant anachronism though he may be in this era of Woodstock. Oliver Goldsmith 3 was counting, 200 years ago, on reader (or playgoer) identification with him; and so vigorous did the type remain that Freud, 1 tracing the dynamic development of the phenomenon, allowed himself to suggest that it might be universal among us, existing as oedipal traces to some degree in any male development. Indeed, if we understand Freud's formulation as describing a special and limiting case of exogamy, then Woodstock notwithstanding, the type is alive and well in the person of Portnoy. 5

But Goldsmith's Marlow and Roth's Portnoy represent at best only half our population. What about the heiress who runs away with the grocery boy? It is evidently a more complex situation than merely the obverse of the other, as one may infer from the fact that nobody has elected to cash in on sure reader identification, and there are no dynamic studies with the cachet of Freud's name to give them luster. The probable explanation of the unequal treatment may lie in the lack of universality. If you've seen one Portnoy, you've seen them all; but every heiress is different.

EDITOR'S NOTE: The Lawrence J. Kaufman Memorial Prize for 1970 was awarded to Dr. Levi for this paper.

I wish to take this opportunity to acknowledge with gratitude my debt to Anna Gourevitch, who over many years has helped me think about children, parents, separateness—and "we."—A.L.

Problems of Creativity

Anthony Storr

Anthony Storr

Anthony Storr, B.Ch.D.P.M.
116 Harley Street
London, W. 1, England

Anthony Storr  

THE SUBJECT of creativity is fraught with paradox. On the one hand, most educated persons give to the artist and his productions as high a value as is accorded to any outstanding person in our culture. On the other, the influence of psychoanalysis has been such that creative activity is regarded as a rather poor substitute for more direct instinctual satisfactions, and the artist as a neurotic whose "real actions are blocked." In an interesting paper called "Freud and the Poet's Eye" 15 Norman Holland points out Freud's own ambivalence towards writers and artists. Freud wrote:

Creative writers are valuable allies and their evidence is to be prized highly, for they are apt to know a whole host of things between heaven and earth of which our philosophy has not yet let us dream. 10

Yet, although Freud admired and envied the insight of the artist, which often arrived by intuition at the same conclusions which he, Freud, could only attain by laborious work, he says in various passages that art and literature are like a child's game, a glorified daydream, a mild narcotic, an illusion offering an escape from reality into fantasy. In the Introductory Lectures, Freud refers to the artist as one

who is urged on by instinctual needs which are too clamorous; he longs to attain to honour, power, riches, fame and the love of women; but he lacks the means of achieving these gratifications. So, like any other with an unsatisfied longing, he turns away from reality and transfers all his interest, and all his libido too, on to the creation of his wishes in the life of phantasy, from which the way might readily lead to neurosis. 11

This paper was delivered as the Presidential Address to the Medical Section, British Psychological Society in 1968.

Key Concepts in Psychotherapy

Erwin Singer. Second edition. New York/London: Basic Books, 1970. 402 pages, $7.50.

Allan Cooper Ph.D.

Allan Cooper

Allan Cooper, Ph.D.
220 Central Park South
New York, N.Y. 10019

Allan Cooper  

THE NEW EDITION of Dr. Singer's book is identical to the 1965 version except for the addition of a new preface and an epilogue on "The Limitation and Danger of Theory in Psychotherapy." With or without those additions, the book is worth reading. It is really a comprehensive comparision of views about the key concepts of psychotherapy. The primary comparison on all issues is between a theory that sees an inherently regressive pull in human nature (Freud) and an orientation toward man's predominant desire to progress, expand, and self-actualize (Sullivan, Rogers, and others).

The book gives extensive coverage to a broad range of significant issues, beginning with the historical and philosophical roots of psychotherapy and then turning to its theoretical and empirical foundations. The author's discussion of these foundations brings the reader into contact with evidence ranging from animal studies to work in extrasensory perception and subliminal perception. Later chapters deal with goals, symptoms, interpretation, resistance, transference, countertransference, and other important topics.

Again and again, Singer summarizes Freud's position on an issue and then compares it to that taken by those who view man as self-actualizing. Although Singer's preference is clear, his book does not impress one as an attack on Freud but rather as a clear comparison of views—an approach which, I believe, is especially valuable for students of psychotherapy. It has been my impression that students being exposed to many teachers or supervisors of various psychoanalytic persuasions learn several positions simultaneously. Because of the similarity, at many points, in the technique of doing therapy, students often do not realize that differences in theoretical positions do exist.

Supervisor of psychotherapy and faculty member, William Alanson White Institute, and assistant clinical professor of psychiatry, New York Medical College.
